chapters.title: The Machine That Learned to See

claims.claim: The Mark I Perceptron was built by psychologist Frank Rosenblatt's project at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo, New York.
The Mark I Perceptron was built by psychologist Frank Rosenblatt's project at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo, New York.
Its 'eye' was a 20 by 20 grid of 400 photocells.
Its adjustable weights were potentiometers turned by electric motors during learning.

In the Mark I the 400 photocells (sensory units) were connected to its association units at random, according to a table of random numbers, through a plugboard (patch board) of cables; the potentiometer arrays that held the adaptive weights stood beside it.
sources: https://americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object/nmah_334414 (read via Smithsonian Open Access API record edanmdm:nmah_334414)

claims.claim: The Mark I Perceptron was not programmed with the rule for telling shapes apart: it was a supervised learning machine, trained by being shown example images and learning by trial and error (its weights corrected when it answered wrongly).
sources: Rosenblatt, F. (1960). Perceptron Simulation Experiments. Proceedings of the IRE 48(3): 301-309.

Rosenblatt, F. (1958). The perceptron: a probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain. Psychological Review 65(6): 386-408. doi:10.1037/h0042519 (read: https://papers.baulab.info/papers/also/Rosenblatt-1958.pdf)

claims.claim: The perceptron learned by error correction: when it answered wrongly, its weights were nudged toward the right answer.
Its adjustable weights were potentiometers turned by electric motors during learning.

A perceptron forms its answer from a weighted sum of its inputs: the total is passed through a threshold (step) function, so a total past the threshold gives one answer and a total short of it the other.
sources: Rosenblatt, F. (1958). The perceptron: a probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain. Psychological Review 65(6): 386-408.

claims.claim: A single-layer perceptron can learn only linearly separable patterns; Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's 1969 book Perceptrons showed that such networks cannot compute functions like XOR, and the book is often thought to have contributed to a decline in neural-network research in the 1970s.

Multilayer perceptrons grew out of efforts to improve on the single-layer perceptron and form the basis of deep learning; like the perceptron, they learn by adjusting connection weights according to the error between their output and the expected result.

In the Mark I the 400 photocells (sensory units) were connected to its association units at random, according to a table of random numbers, through a plugboard (patch board) of cables; the potentiometer arrays that held the adaptive weights stood beside it.
